source.title: SARSteer: Safeguarding Large Audio Language Models via Safe-Ablated Refusal Steering
source.authors: Weilin Lin; Jianze Li; Hui Xiong; Li Liu

record.file_problem: The full paper and supplementary material are present. Some figure text is garbled and some tables are flattened, but the relevant table values are assignable.
record.tranche_reason: The study extends activation steering to large audio-language models and reports behavioral outcomes. It tests audio adaptations of difference-in-means steering and tests a text-derived refusal vector in audio models, but it does not reproduce the original all-layer, all-position ablation.
record.gate_note: The paper also reports prompt-defense comparisons and hyperparameter sweeps. Those are not included unless their result directly bears on steering transfer or refusal behavior. The CKA and t-SNE analyses explain modality differences but do not directly measure refusal behavior.
record.test_reason: The study adds difference-in-means steering vectors (harmful-vs-safe and compliance-vs-refusal, computed from audio inputs) to audio-language models and measures harmful-query compliance by LLM-judged ASR. That is a new setting for V1's addition test. The original all-layer, all-position ablation is not run. SARSteer, the paper's own method, uses a different vector (activations with an appended refusal sentence minus without, PCA-projected). Its results are the method's performance, not a test of any version.
record.authors_conclusion: Mostly right. The authors conclude that difference-in-means steering computed from audio inputs fails, and often worsens ASR, because harmful and safe audio activations are separated at all layers. They report that a refusal vector derived from text with its safe-subspace component removed (SARSteer) reduces harmful compliance without over-refusal or utility loss. They do not note that their harmful-to-safe vector is the negated refusal direction.
record.recipe_differences: Instead of projecting out the original difference-in-means refusal direction at every layer and position and testing both removal and addition, the study tests audio-adapted harmful-to-safe and compliance-to-refusal steering and proposes a text-prompt-derived vector with PCA safe-subspace projection. The interventions are applied during inference in audio-language models.
record.method_sensitivity: Results vary by steering formulation, model, and dataset. The paper reports that vanilla harmful-safe and compliance-refusal audio steering can worsen ASR; SARSteer’s outcome also varies by dataset and checkpoint. For SARSteer, α controls the ASR/BRR tradeoff, while the reported curves are described as relatively flat across the tested sample counts and PCA component counts.

fits_no_version.finding: A steering vector built from activations with an appended refusal sentence minus without, with a PCA safe subspace projected out, lowers ASR in seven audio-language models, a base audio model and text-only Qwen2. Benign refusal stays at or below 1.6%, and AirBench utility is roughly unchanged.
fits_no_version.proposed_claim: A refusal-prompt-derived activation vector, orthogonalised against a benign subspace, induces refusal of harmful audio queries without over-refusal.

record.peer_reviewed: Proceedings of the 43rd International Conference on Machine Learning, PMLR 306, 2026
record.problems: The original all-layer, all-position ablation is not tested. The main harmfulness metric is LLM-judged ASR; the paper reports a human check on 500 stratified samples and describes conservative judge bias. Main paired-set steering uses 100 sampled pairs. BRR is an aggregate and does not isolate benign-query refusal; Safe RR is separately reported only for the three newer models. Primary table results generally lack uncertainty intervals.
record.rows_left_out: Omitted prompt-defense results, SARSteer results for additional datasets/checkpoints beyond those retained, hyperparameter sweeps, fine-tuning comparisons, and attack-condition results in Tables 5–18 and Appendix B. These were not necessary to cover the tested versions within the 60-row limit; the retained rows prioritize difference-in-means steering outcomes and text-derived steering transfer.

untested.parts: Directional ablation at all layers and positions; the exact harmful-minus-harmless direction added to induce refusal on harmless inputs (only the negated harmful-to-safe vector and a refusal-minus-compliance vector are added, at α=0.1, at last-token-derived layers); text-input models.
Not tested: no weight edit or abliteration.
Not tested: attacks are not analysed in terms of the direction, and there is no adversarial training against ablation.
Not tested: no direction is transferred across languages, model variants, or base/instruct; each vector is computed in the model where it is applied.

missing.what: MDSteer-h2s and MDSteer-c2r ASR on Qwen2-Audio-Base. h2s: 62.8→45.6, 49.77→16.82, 43.0→18.5, 51.15→20.77. c2r: 46.4, 22.5, 28.0, 19.23. Both lower ASR on the base model, unlike on the instruct models.

MDSteer-h2s and MDSteer-c2r ASR and benign Safe RR on three newer audio models. h2s ASR: 42→58.8, 7.2→62.8, 34→50.8, with Safe RR 0.0% on all. c2r ASR: 52.3, 15.2, 26.8, with Safe RR 0.8/2.0/0.8%. So the refusal-ward vector does not induce benign refusal.
AirBench average utility under MDSteer: Qwen2-Audio 7.32 (h2s) and 7.44 (c2r) vs 7.43; Kimi-Audio 7.21 and 7.20 vs 7.20. Utility is kept under addition.
CKA of harmful vs safe hidden states: audio 0.063 vs text 0.672 (linear). The authors' explanation for steering failure in audio.

record.verdict_notes: Sign issue: Eq.4 defines v_h2s = µsafe − µharm and adds it during generation. By Arditi et al.'s convention this pushes away from refusal, so rising ASR under h2s matches V1 rather than showing failure; the authors frame it as failure. The c2r vector (refused minus complied) is the one whose addition should induce refusal, and it raised ASR. All vectors are computed from audio inputs at the last token with α=0.1, a small scale, and the layer choice is unclear. ASR comes from a Mistral judge that human checks show is biased toward flagging unsafe (43 false positives vs 3 false negatives). MDSteer refusal rates on benign inputs are not reported for the main models. The SARSteer rows are own-method results and were unlinked from V6.

versions.untested_parts: Tests addition of audio-adapted difference-in-means steering vectors, not removal of the original direction from every layer and position. It does not isolate whether adding that original direction induces refusals to harmless requests, and it does not test the original direction’s general-capability cost.
No weight-edit or released-model abliteration experiment.
Adaptive attacks are evaluated, but they are not shown to suppress the refusal direction; the paper does not train against that direction’s ablation.
No test of affine, cone, or multiple-direction accounts of refusal.
No separation of harmfulness judgment from the refusal decision.
Tests transfer to audio models, model variants, and a base model, but not transfer across languages.
The base-model experiment evaluates the proposed defense, not whether training determines the existence of a removable refusal direction.

relationships.condition: Qwen2-Audio and Kimi-Audio, adding the audio harmful-to-safe vector (the negated difference-in-means direction), α=0.1
relationships.reason: Adding µsafe−µharm raised ASR on 7 of 8 model-benchmark pairs (e.g. 15.6→72.4), consistent with the sign of the refusal direction; the authors instead read this as steering failure (r1, r2, r4, r13-r16).
relationships.display_finding: Adding the safe-minus-harmful vector at α=0.1 increased attack success on seven of eight model-benchmark pairs, including an increase from 15.6 to 72.4.

source_check.label: supports
source_check.condition: Qwen2-Audio and Kimi-Audio, adding the audio harmful-to-safe vector (the negated difference-in-means direction), α=0.1
source_check.reason: The numbers fit the sign: µsafe − µharm raised ASR on 7 of 8 pairs (r1, r2, r4, r13–r16), and Table 14 shows rises on three more LALMs. But the refusal-ward c2r vector also raised ASR, and by more than h2s on 3 of 4 Qwen2-Audio benchmarks (90.80 vs 84.00, 78.41 vs 75.45, 49.00 vs 38.50). tranche.reason: It adds difference-in-means vectors computed from audio inputs (h2s: harmful vs safe paired audio, i.e. V1's contrast with the sign negated) to audio-language models and reports LLM-judged ASR against a no-defense baseline. That is a new setting with a result on V1.

source_check.notes: The steering baselines use α=0.1 and n=100 Figstep-audio pairs, with vectors computed at the last token and added at every generated position. Table 14 (newer LALMs, Figstep-audio) gives h2s 42.0→58.8, 7.2→62.8, 34.0→50.8 and c2r 42.0→52.3, 7.2→15.2, 34.0→26.8; these are not in the checked rows. The ASR judge is a fine-tuned Mistral-7B, and its human check (B.11) shows a conservative bias (43 of 500 labelled unsafe that humans judged safe). SARSteer's own vector (prompt + refusal text minus prompt) is not V1's contrast.

statements.correction: Qwen2-Audio c2r: 51.60→90.80 (Figstep), 27.50→78.41 (SORRY), 48.76→49.00 (AJailBench), 2.88→23.46 (AdvBench). Qwen2-Audio-Base (Table 8): c2r lowers ASR 62.80→46.40, 49.77→22.50, 43.00→28.00, 51.15→19.23; h2s also lowers all four. Voxtral-Mini-3B c2r: Figstep 34.0→26.8 (Table 14). The statement also leaves out that the same vectors lower ASR on the base model and on Voxtral, and that the authors blame the audio modality gap.
